title: In fly, mouse and human data, surrogate wiring with matched node strengths and distances reproduced 48-100% of the FC gain of indirect-path measures; a large specific gain stayed only in sedated mouse
abstract: We tested if indirect structural paths predict functional connectivity (FC) between brain regions beyond direct wiring. We used four data sets: fly hemibrain wiring with 2-photon FC (20 flies), FlyWire wiring with light-field FC (48 flies), the Allen mouse tracer model with resting fMRI (79 mice), and human diffusion MRI with resting fMRI (50 people). We added six communication measures (shortest path, search information, communicability, diffusion, two-step weight, connection-profile similarity) to cross-validated pair models with distance and direct wiring, and then with one fixed effect per region. We compared the real gains with gains from surrogate wiring that keeps the weights, the distance law and the node strengths (40-200 surrogates). Over distance and direct wiring, the measures increased cross-validated R2 in all data sets (0.131, 0.067, 0.045, 0.021 per individual), but the surrogates gave 76%, 57%, 48% and 100% of this gain. Region effects without any wiring explained more FC than distance plus direct wiring in flies and human. After region effects, the gain specific to the real paths was small in flies and human (0.008, 0.005, 0.003; surrogate p 0.005-0.022) and larger in mouse (0.031). In the same mice, this mouse gain was 0.033 under medetomidine plus isoflurane, but 0.008 under isoflurane alone (10 mice, p = 0.002) and awake (6 mice, p = 0.031). Walking did not change the fly gain. Limitations: region scale only; the mouse wiring is a smoothed tracer model; mouse and human have only 40-45 surrogates; node effects can absorb real hub communication.
